A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main texts, figures, tables, equations and complete Appendices A–H support comparison. Internal reporting inconsistencies do not prevent identifying the changes.

before.justification: v1 reports original supervised and MuJoCo experiments, activation-slope sweeps, shock-recovery measurements and generalization analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds comparator evaluations, continual-learning intervention experiments and supplementary activation results.

M1.justification: The Smooth-Leaky and Randomized Smooth-Leaky formulas and inference rules remain unchanged. Bo-PReLU and RSELU were already defined in v1 Appendix G. The added regularization/reset experiments evaluate interventions with the retained activation designs.

E1.justification: The versions use the same Split-CIFAR-100 study, five supervised benchmarks, scaling-shock scenarios and MuJoCo/friction evaluations. Humanoid-v5 already appears in v1’s RL tables. Added analyses and intervention arms reuse this coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated SwiGLU and Deep Fourier Features comparators to the supervised and RL comparisons (Tables 2 and F1). Appendix E.3 additionally compares vanilla activations with L2-Init, Self-Normalized Resets and EWC across all five supervised benchmarks, substantially broadening the comparison methods.

E3.justification: Table B1 expands reported activation-parameter sweeps. Section 7 replaces raw-return median-based Plasticity Scores with normalized, failure-clipped IQM scoring and changes gap aggregation/filtering. Table F1 changes the selected randomized Smooth-Leaky RL bounds from [0.01,0.1] to [0.01,0.02]. New supervised gap evaluations and intervention grids add protocols; these reported changes do not establish which existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendices E.2–E.3 test supervised generalization and whether activation advantages persist with regularization or neuron resets. Tables G2–G3 empirically test the previously defined Bo-PReLU and RSELU variants. Existing slope and correlation analyses are also expanded; the relocated dead-band analysis was already present in v1.

E5.justification: v2 adds standard deviations to existing accuracy results in Tables 1–2, confidence intervals to RL gap results, and explicitly identifies Welch’s tests for supervised comparisons. It also adopts IQM aggregation. Both versions report five runs/seeds for the principal comparisons; there is no stated increase in that count.

E6.justification: Substantial new results cover interventions, supervised gaps, raw RL returns and supplementary activations. In Table 2, newly evaluated Deep Fourier Features leads CIFAR 5+1 with 72.29%, above the retained randomized Smooth-Leaky result of 57.01%. Rational’s Random Label MNIST value changes from 91.27% to 92.35%. Correlation results and RL summaries also change; the revised RL scores are not directly comparable performance gains.

T1.justification: Section 7 substantively redefines Plasticity Score through normalization, clipping and IQM aggregation. Appendix E.2 introduces the supervised gap definition using final test accuracy minus average online training accuracy. Activation equations and curvature definitions remain unchanged, and neither version supplies theoretical proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, principal contribution list and conclusion retain the same scientific claims: activation design supports plasticity, moderate negative responsiveness and narrow dead bands guide design, and two drop-in nonlinearities improve continual adaptation. The additional evidence does not redefine these core contributions.

C2.justification: v1 interprets the randomized activation’s extremely negative Humanoid gap favorably; v2 identifies simulation failures and qualifies transfer benefits by environment stability. New discussion addresses Adam-specific scope, Deep Fourier Features’ generalization tradeoffs, and circumstances where regularization helps or harms adaptation (Appendices B.1 and E.2–E.3).

D1.justification: v2 explicitly identifies Adam and documents intervention implementation, parameter grids and per-activation settings in Tables E9–E11, including SNR thresholds/window size and EWC decay. Tables E2, F1 and G4 supply settings for added comparisons and supplementary activation experiments. The code-access link remains unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds references and positioning concerning Deep Fourier Features, SwiGLU and its language-model usage, SNR, EWC, Adam and robust RL aggregation. These extend the existing activation/plasticity discussion without replacing its central novelty positioning.

P1.justification: Localized rewrites revise the slope-failure and RL narratives, integrate existing appendix explanations into the main text, and introduce additional appendix subsections and acknowledgments. The abstract, overall section sequence, activation descriptions and much of the existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 consolidates and redraws v1 Figures C1–C2 as main-text Figure 1 and moves the dead-band analysis into Figure 4. It expands primary tables with uncertainty, updates plots and the RL heatmap, and adds extensive tables for supervised gaps, interventions, raw RL rewards and Appendix G experiments.

improvement.justification: Added uncertainty, stronger comparisons, intervention tests and explicit recognition of physics failures improve evidential transparency over v1. However, the expanded evidence is imperfectly reconciled with the narrative: Table 2 shows Deep Fourier Features winning CIFAR 5+1 despite text saying it trails the proposed variants, and Tables 4/F3 disagree on the sign of randomized Smooth-Leaky’s gap IQM (59.03 versus -59.03). These inconsistencies limit confidence in the revised conclusions.
